claim: Beta oscillations (15-29Hz) are among the most prominent signatures of brain activity.
source: Beta oscillations (15-29Hz) are among the most prominent signatures of brain activity.
evidence: This is a general statement about beta oscillations supported by established scientific knowledge and the literature cited throughout the manuscript.

claim: Beta power is predictive of healthy and abnormal behaviors, including perception, attention and motor action.
source: Beta power is predictive of healthy and abnormal behaviors, including perception, attention and motor action.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature throughout the manuscript and is part of established scientific knowledge.

claim: In non-averaged signals, beta can emerge as transient high-power 'events'.
source: In non-averaged signals, beta can emerge as transient high-power 'events'.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2 showing individual trial spectrograms.

claim: Functionally relevant differences in averaged beta power in primary somatosensory neocortex reflect a difference in the number of high-power beta events per trial (event rate).
source: We show that functionally relevant differences in averaged beta power in primary somatosensory neocortex reflect a difference in the number of high-power beta events per trial, i.e. event rate.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figures 6 and 7 showing correlations and behavioral predictions.

claim: Beta events occurring close to the stimulus were more likely to impair perception.
source: Further, beta events occurring close to the stimulus were more likely to impair perception.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 8 showing timing relationships between beta events and detection.

claim: These results are consistent across detection and attention tasks in human magnetoencephalography.
source: These results are consistent across detection and attention tasks in human magnetoencephalography, and in local field potentials from mice performing a detection task.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented across multiple figures (Figures 1, 6, 7, 8) for both human MEG detection and attention tasks.

claim: These results are consistent in local field potentials from mice performing a detection task.
source: These results are consistent across detection and attention tasks in human magnetoencephalography, and in local field potentials from mice performing a detection task.
evidence: This claim is supported by mouse LFP data presented in Figures 1B, 6B, 7B, and 8B.

claim: An increased propensity of beta events predicts the failure to effectively transmit information through specific neocortical representations.
source: These results imply that an increased propensity of beta events predicts the failure to effectively transmit information through specific neocortical representations.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data showing negative correlations between beta event rate and detection/attention performance.

claim: Modulations in beta power correlate with perceptual and motor demands.
source: Modulations in beta power correlate with perceptual and motor demands (Bauer et al., 2006; Bressler and Richter, 2015; Engel and Fries, 2010; Haegens et al., 2011; Jones et al., 2010; Miller et al., 2012; Neuper and Pfurtscheller, 2001; Sacchet et al., 2015; Siegel et al., 2008; van Ede et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Abnormalities in beta are a biomarker for neuropathology (e.g. in Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease and Autism Spectrum Disorder).
source: abnormalities in beta are a biomarker for neuropathology (e.g. in Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease and Autism Spectrum Disorder [Karageorgiou and Vossel, 2017; Khan et al., 2015; Little and Brown, 2014]).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on beta abnormalities in disease.

claim: High power beta frequency activity (15–29 Hz) emerges as brief events typically lasting <150 ms.
source: In such studies, high power beta frequency activity (15–29 Hz) emerges as brief events typically lasting <150 ms.
evidence: This claim is supported by prior studies cited and by data in Figure 5 showing event duration distributions.

claim: Transient beta has been reported in many brain areas including somatosensory, motor, occipital, and frontal neocortex, and basal ganglia structures.
source: Transient beta has been reported in many brain areas including somatosensory (Jones et al., 2009; Sherman et al., 2016; Ziegler et al., 2010), motor (Feingold et al., 2015; Rule et al., 2017), occipital (Freyer et al., 2009), and frontal neocortex (Lundqvist et al., 2016; Sherman et al., 2016), and basal ganglia structures (Bartolo and Merchant, 2015; Feingold et al., 2015; Tinkhauser et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Transient beta has been reported across recording modalities and species.
source: and across recording modalities and species (Sherman et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Differences in the accumulated density of transient beta bursts across trials predicts functionally relevant differences in averaged beta power reflecting motor and cognitive demands in monkey local field potentials (LFP) data.
source: Further, differences in the accumulated density of transient beta bursts across trials predicts functionally relevant differences in averaged beta power reflecting motor and cognitive demands in monkey local field potentials (LFP) data (Feingold et al., 2015; Lundqvist et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies in monkeys.

claim: Lower prestimulus beta power (averaged in the 1 s prestimulus time window) in the human primary somatosensory neocortex (SI) predicts an increase in the probability of detection of tactile stimuli at perceptual threshold.
source: We have previously shown, using magnetoencephalography (MEG), that lower prestimulus beta power (averaged in the 1 s prestimulus time window) in the human primary somatosensory neocortex (SI) predicts an increase in the probability of detection of tactile stimuli at perceptual threshold (Jones et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and by data in Figure 1A.

claim: Shifts in spatial attention modulate post-cue/prestimulus beta power, such that average power decreases in the attended SI location.
source: Correspondingly, shifts in spatial attention modulate post-cue/prestimulus beta power, such that average power decreases in the attended SI location (Jones et al., 2010; Sacchet et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and by data in Figure 1C.

claim: A lower rate of prestimulus beta events predicts enhanced detection of stimuli at perceptual threshold.
source: A lower rate of prestimulus beta events predicts enhanced detection of stimuli at perceptual threshold
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 7 showing event rate relationships with detection.

claim: The rate of beta events in the attended region of the brain decreases.
source: and the rate of beta events in the attended region of the brain decreases.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 7C showing event rate in attention task.

claim: Non-detected trials were more likely to have a high-power beta event within approximately 200 ms of the stimulus.
source: Moreover, non-detected trials were more likely to have a high-power beta event within approximately 200 ms of the stimulus.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 8 showing timing relationships.

claim: Beta events were not a byproduct of a sustained oscillation whose power gets dynamically modulated.
source: Importantly, these beta events were not a byproduct a sustained oscillation whose power gets dynamically modulated
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 12 comparing dynamic amplitude modulation vs. bursty generator hypotheses.

claim: Beta events may be generated by a transient, 'bursty' mechanism.
source: rather, we find evidence that beta events may be generated by a transient, 'bursty' mechanism.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figures 10, 11, and 12 showing non-rhythmic event generation and support for bursty generator hypothesis.

claim: Differences in the rate and timing of 'bursty' beta events underlie the correlation between beta power and behavior in humans.
source: These results show that differences in the rate and timing of 'bursty' beta events underlie the correlation between beta power and behavior in humans.
evidence: This is a summary inference drawn from the data presented in Figures 6-9.

claim: Results were remarkably consistent in LFP recordings from awake behaving mice performing a similar tactile detection task.
source: Results were remarkably consistent in LFP recordings from awake behaving mice performing a similar tactile detection task.
evidence: This claim is supported by mouse data presented throughout the results section (Figures 1B, 2B, 4B, 5B, 6B, 7B, 8B, etc.).

claim: The strong parallel in the character of beta events across behavior, recording scales, and species indicates a fundamental consistency in the nature of this much-studied dynamic in the mammalian neocortex.
source: The strong parallel in the character of beta events across behavior, recording scales, and species indicates a fundamental consistency in the nature of this much-studied dynamic in the mammalian neocortex.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the consistency of results across human MEG and mouse LFP data.

claim: The rate of detection (hit rate, measured as percent change from mean [PCM]) decreases as averaged prestimulus beta power increases.
source: Figure 1Aii illustrates this result, showing that the rate of detection (hit rate, measured as percent change from mean [PCM]) decreases as averaged prestimulus beta power increases.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by data shown in Figure 1Aii.

claim: Beta power plotted as a function of time was higher on non-detected trials throughout the prestimulus window.
source: Further, beta power plotted as a function of time was higher on non-detected trials throughout the prestimulus window (Figure 1Ai).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by data shown in Figure 1Ai.

claim: Human detection data were obtained from an MEG dipole source localized to the contralateral hand area of SI in the post-central gyrus in all subjects (N = 10 subjects).
source: Human detection data were obtained from an MEG dipole source localized to the contralateral hand area of SI in the post-central gyrus in all subjects (N = 10 subjects), see Figure 1—figure supplement 1A for the evoked response and further details in the Materials and methods.
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the data source.

claim: Beta power recorded as LFP from SI of mice performing a similar vibrissae task also shows a negative relationship to detection.
source: Beta power recorded as LFP from SI of mice performing a similar vibrissae task (Figure 1Bi–ii) also shows a negative relationship to detection.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1Bi-ii.

claim: Mouse LFP data were obtained from the SI 'barrel' neocortex contralateral to the stimulated vibrissae (N = 10 sessions from two mice).
source: These data were obtained from the SI 'barrel' neocortex contralateral to the stimulated vibrissae (N = 10 sessions from two mice), see Figure 1—figure supplement 1A for evoked response and further details in the Materials and methods.
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the data source.

claim: When human subjects are cued to attend to perceptual-threshold level stimulation in the hand or foot, a similar negative relationship exists between prestimulus beta power and the allocation of attention (attend-in rate, measured as PCM of attend hand trial).
source: Consistent with this prediction, when human subjects are cued to attend to perceptual-threshold level stimulation in the hand or foot (Jones et al., 2010; Sacchet et al., 2015), a similar negative relationship exists between prestimulus beta power and the allocation of attention (attend-in rate, measured as PCM of attend hand trial) (Figure 1Ci–ii; analysis was limited to detected trials to compare the effect of attention independent of detection).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1Ci-ii and citations to prior work.

claim: Human attention data were obtained from a MEG dipole source localized to the contralateral hand area of SI (N = 10 subjects).
source: Human attention data were also obtained from a MEG dipole source localized to the contralateral hand area of SI (N = 10 subjects, see further details in Materials and methods and Jones et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the data source.

claim: All three datasets showed significance, such that the pooled average was significantly higher on non-detected/attend out trials (p<0.05, right-tailed paired t-test).
source: All three datasets showed significance, such that the pooled average was significantly higher on non-detected/attend out trials (p<0.05, right-tailed paired t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 1iii.

claim: The difference across behavioral conditions was larger for detection than attention (see Cohen's d values in Figure 1 panels iii).
source: Quantification of the corresponding effect size showed the difference across behavioral conditions was larger for detection than attention (see Cohen's d values in Figure 1 panels iii).
evidence: This claim is supported by effect size calculations shown in Figure 1iii.

claim: In all three datasets, the median of DP and AP distributions were significantly <0.5, such that higher power indicated the subject was less likely to detect or attend to the stimulus.
source: In all three datasets, the median of DP and AP distributions were significantly <0.5, such that higher power indicated the subject was less likely to detect or attend to the stimulus (Figure 1iv asterisks p<0.05, p-values from one-sample left-tailed Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 1iv.

claim: The effect was stronger in the detection datasets, where in 50% of human subjects and mouse sessions high beta was significantly predictive of non-detection, as compared to the attention dataset where only 10% of the subjects showed significance.
source: While this effect was significant in all three datasets, the effect was stronger in the detection datasets, where in 50% of human subjects and mouse sessions high beta was significantly predictive of non-detection, as compared to the attention dataset where only 10% of the subjects showed significance (Figure 1iv, see parentheses above each plot, bootstrapped 1000 times to determine 95% confidence interval for each subject/session. DP/AP is significantly less than 0.5 if the upper boundary of the bootstrapped confidence interval is less than 0.5).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 1iv.

claim: Averaged beta power was not significantly higher in correct rejections compared to false alarms across sessions, arguing strongly against the possibility that the difference was due to modulation of the criterion or motor readiness.
source: Averaged beta power was not significantly higher in correct rejections compared to false alarms across sessions, arguing strongly against the possibility that the difference was due to modulation of the criterion or motor readiness (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B; right-tailed paired t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Beta emerges as a transient surge in power (i.e. events) on individual trials in our data.
source: Beta emerges as a transient surge in power (i.e. events) on individual trials in our data (Figure 2ii).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2ii showing individual trial spectrograms.

claim: The accumulation of events across trials creates a continuous band of activity in the average, often misinterpreted as a sustained rhythm.
source: Because power spectral values are non-negative, the accumulation of events across trials creates a continuous band of activity in the average, often misinterpreted as a sustained rhythm (Figure 2i) (Jones, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of averaged (Figure 2i) and individual trial (Figure 2ii) spectrograms, and by citation.

claim: This observation holds across tasks and species.
source: We find that this observation holds across tasks and species (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2 for all three datasets.

claim: The correlation with mean power was highest near the 6X median power cutoff across species and behavioral tasks.
source: The correlation with mean power was highest near the 6X median power cutoff across species and behavioral tasks (dotted line in Figure 4i).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4i.

claim: This power cutoff best accounted for the variability in trial mean prestimulus power.
source: In other words, this power cutoff best accounted for the variability in trial mean prestimulus power, the effect we are seeking to understand.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation analysis shown in Figure 4i.

claim: 6X median cutoff captures ~20% of all local maxima.
source: The inverse cumulative density function (1-CDF) of all local maxima in the beta band as a function of the power cutoff shows that 6X median cutoff captures ~20% of all local maxima (Figure 4ii).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4ii.

claim: There was homology in the distribution of beta event features across tasks and species.
source: There was homology in the distribution of beta event features across tasks and species
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of distributions shown in Figure 5 across all three datasets.

claim: In almost all trials, <4 beta events occurred in the 1 s prestimulus period.
source: In almost all trials,<4 beta events occurred in the 1 s prestimulus period
evidence: This claim is supported by event number distributions shown in Figure 5.

claim: The event power probability histogram fell off monotonically after the power cutoff.
source: the event power probability histogram fell off monotonically after the power cutoff
evidence: This claim is supported by event power distributions shown in Figure 5.

claim: The event duration was confined to a restricted range around a stereotypical value (mean ±SEM across events: human detection 167 ± 1.6 ms; mouse detection 145 ± 1.3 ms; human attention 153 ± 1.4 ms).
source: the event duration was confined to a restricted range around a stereotypical value (mean ±SEM across events: human detection 167 ± 1.6 ms; mouse detection 145 ± 1.3 ms; human attention 153 ± 1.4 ms)
evidence: This claim is supported by event duration distributions shown in Figure 5 and statistical calculations.

claim: The event frequency span was confined around a stereotypical value (mean ±SEM across events: human detection 8.6 ± 0.07 Hz; mouse detection 10.6 ± 0.11 Hz; human attention 8.9 ± 0.07 Hz).
source: and, the event frequency span was confined around a stereotypical value (mean ±SEM across events: human detection 8.6 ± 0.07 Hz; mouse detection 10.6 ± 0.11 Hz; human attention 8.9 ± 0.07 Hz).
evidence: This claim is supported by event frequency span distributions shown in Figure 5 and statistical calculations.

claim: Below the 6X median threshold, event duration and frequency span become more distributed.
source: Below the 6X median threshold, event duration and frequency span become more distributed (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was consistency across species and tasks in the correlation coefficient distributions.
source: Again, there was consistency across species and tasks.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of correlation distributions shown in Figure 6 across all three datasets.

claim: In each dataset, the number of beta events in the prestimulus period (i.e. rate) showed a significantly higher correlation with trial mean prestimulus beta power than the trial mean event power, duration or frequency span.
source: In each dataset, the number of beta events in the prestimulus period (i.e. rate) showed a significantly higher correlation with trial mean prestimulus beta power than the trial mean event power, duration or frequency span (Figure 6 asterisks denote p<0.05, Holm-Bonferroni corrected post-hoc Wilcoxon signed rank test; see also Figure 6—figure supplement 1 for scatterplots of example subject data and Figure 6—figure supplement 2 for variations in power cutoff).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The number of beta events in the prestimulus period was also the most consistent predictor of behavior across datasets.
source: The number of beta events in the prestimulus period was also the most consistent predictor of behavior across datasets.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Prestimulus beta event rate mirrors the beta power, where the event rate is higher in non-detected compared to detected trials throughout most of the 1 s prestimulus window.
source: Figure 7i shows that prestimulus beta event rate mirrors the beta power (Figure 1i), where the event rate is higher in non-detected compared to detected trials throughout most of the 1 s prestimulus window.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7i.

claim: In the human data, only the number of events per trial was significantly higher in non-detected (miss)/attend out conditions.
source: In the human data, only the number of events per trial was significantly higher in non-detected (miss)/attend out conditions (Figure 7iii, asterisks p<0.05, right-tailed paired t-test)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 7iii.

claim: Only the number of events had DP/AP distributions that were significantly less than 0.5 across subjects.
source: and only the number of events had DP/AP distributions that were significantly less than 0.5 across subjects (Figure 7iv, asterisks p<0.05, one-sample left-tailed Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 7iv.

claim: The number of beta events was also predictive of behavior in the mouse LFP.
source: The number of beta events was also predictive of behavior in the mouse LFP.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: In the mouse dataset, trial mean event power and frequency span were also predictive of non-detection, possibly due to the different signal to noise ratio stemming from the different recording modalities.
source: In this dataset, trial mean event power and frequency span were also predictive of non-detection, possibly due to the different signal to noise ratio stemming from the different recording modalities.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7B and is a speculation about the cause.

claim: In all three datasets, the effect size of the difference across behavioral conditions was higher for event number than any other event feature.
source: However, in all three datasets, the effect size of the difference across behavioral conditions was higher for event number than any other event feature (see Cohen's d values in Figure 7iii).
evidence: This claim is supported by effect size calculations shown in Figure 7iii.

claim: The percent of subjects/sessions that had DP/AP significantly less than 0.5 was highest for event number in all three datasets.
source: Further, the percent of subjects/sessions that had DP/AP significantly less than 0.5 was highest for event number in all three datasets (as determined by 95% confidence interval, constructed from bootstrapping 1000 times; see parentheses Figure 7iv).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 7iv.

claim: The event number (i.e. rate) was the most consistent predictor of behavior across tasks and species.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the event number (i.e. rate) was the most consistent predictor of behavior across tasks and species.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data presented in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Trials with zero events were more likely to be detected, and trials with two or more events were more likely not to be detected.
source: These distributions and the corresponding effect size values in Figure 7—figure supplement 2D suggest that trials with zero events were more likely to be detected, and trials with two or more events were more likely not to be detected.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Trials with zero events were slightly more likely in the attend-in condition, and trials with two or more events occurred more often in the attend-out condition.
source: Trials with zero events were slightly more likely in the attend-in condition, and trials with two or more events occurred more often in the attend-out condition.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: In each dataset, the optimal event number criterion was two events for most subjects/sessions (60% of subjects in human and mouse detection, and 50% of subjects in human attention).
source: Consistent with the distributions and effect sizes, in each dataset, the optimal event number criterion was two events for most subjects/sessions (Figure 7–figure supplement 2ii; 60% of subjects in human and mouse detection, and 50% of subjects in human attention).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2ii.

claim: Trials with ≥2 prestimulus events predict non-detection/attend out conditions and trials with 0 events predict detection/attend in conditions, while trials with one event are not predictive without additional information about event features.
source: Put another way, trials with ≥2 prestimulus events predict non-detection/attend out conditions and trials with 0 events predict detection/attend in conditions, while trials with one event are not predictive without additional information about event features.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the optimal criterion analysis.

claim: In trials with one event, the event timing was significantly closer to stimulus onset on non-detected trials across human detection subjects, and trended towards significance (p<0.1) in the mouse detection sessions.
source: We found that in trials with one event, the event timing was significantly closer to stimulus onset on non-detected trials across human detection subjects, and trended towards significance (p<0.1) in the mouse detection sessions (right-tailed paired t-test, Figure 7–figure supplement 2iii, A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2iii.

claim: We would not expect a difference in timing relative to the stimulus onset in the different attention conditions, as the timing of the attentional cue relative to the stimulus onset was randomized.
source: We would not expect a difference in timing relative to the stimulus onset in the different attention conditions, as the timing of the attentional cue relative to the stimulus onset was randomized (confirmed in Figure 7–figure supplement 2Ciii).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design, confirmed by data in Figure 7—figure supplement 2Ciii.

claim: For any number of events in the prestimulus period, the timing of the beta event occurring closest to stimulus onset (i.e. 'most recent beta event') mattered for detection.
source: Based on these results, we hypothesized that, for any number of events in the prestimulus period, the timing of the beta event occurring closest to stimulus onset (i.e. 'most recent beta event') mattered for detection.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the data showing timing effects in single-event trials.

claim: Beta events were more likely to happen closer to stimulus onset on non-detected trials.
source: The probability time histogram of the 'most recent beta event' per trial showed that beta events were more likely to happen closer to stimulus onset on non-detected trials (Figure 8i).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8i.

claim: The probability time histogram profiles were significantly different out to ~200 ms prestimulus in the human and mouse data, suggesting that beta events' influence on function may have an effective period that lasts about ~200 ms.
source: The probability time histogram profiles were significantly different out to ~200 ms prestimulus in the human and mouse data, suggesting that beta events' influence on function may have an effective period that lasts about ~200 ms (pointwise left-tailed Wilcoxon signed rank test, p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 8i and is an inference about the functional impact.

claim: In the human data, the 'most recent beta event' timing (relative to the stimulus onset) was the only significant feature, such that the closer the 'most recent beta event' was to the stimulus the less likely the subject was to detect.
source: In the human data, the 'most recent beta event' timing (relative to the stimulus onset) was the only significant feature, such that the closer the 'most recent beta event' was to the stimulus the less likely the subject was to detect (Figure 8Aii-iv; right-tailed paired t-test comparing the pooled average between behavioral conditions, and one-sample left-tailed Wilcoxon signed rank test of the DP distribution).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: In the mouse data, the timing of the 'most recent beta event' predicted detection as well.
source: In the mouse data, the timing of the 'most recent beta event' predicted detection as well (Figure 8Bii-iv).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: As in Figure 7Biii-iv, 'most recent beta event' power and frequency span also showed significance in the mouse data.
source: As in Figure 7Biii-iv, 'most recent beta event' power and frequency span also showed significance in the mouse data.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The effect size was consistently highest for 'most recent beta event' timing in humans and mice.
source: However, the effect size was consistently highest for 'most recent beta event' timing in humans and mice (Figure 8iii)
evidence: This claim is supported by effect size calculations shown in Figure 8iii.

claim: The percent of subjects/sessions with DP significantly less than 0.5 was highest for 'most recent beta event' timing.
source: and the percent of subjects/sessions with DP significantly less than 0.5 was highest for 'most recent beta event' timing (as determined by 95% confidence interval, constructed from bootstrapping 1000 times; see parentheses Figure 8iv).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 8iv.

claim: The timing of the 'most recent beta event' influenced detection more consistently than its power, duration or frequency span.
source: Hence, the timing of the 'most recent beta event' influenced detection more consistently than its power, duration or frequency span.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data presented in Figure 8.

claim: As the cutoff was lowered below ~3X median, the 'most recent event' power had a more significant influence on perception than the timing relative to the stimulus onset.
source: Variation of the power cutoff defining beta events for features of the 'most recent beta event' revealed similarities between timing and event number. As the cutoff was lowered below ~3X median, the 'most recent event' power had a more significant influence on perception than the timing relative to the stimulus onset (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The pooled average of 'most recent beta event' timing was significantly closer to stimulus onset on non-detected trials in the human detection dataset (right-tailed paired t-test, p=0.01) and trended toward significance in the mouse detection dataset (p=0.076).
source: The pooled average of 'most recent beta event' timing was significantly closer to stimulus onset on non-detected trials in the human detection dataset (right-tailed paired t-test, p=0.01) and trended toward significance in the mouse detection dataset (p=0.076).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of event number matched data shown in Figure 9i.

claim: These results provide support for the hypothesis that the 'most recent beta event' timing can be predictive of detection independent of event number.
source: These results provide support for the hypothesis that the 'most recent beta event' timing can be predictive of detection independent of event number.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the event number matching analysis shown in Figure 9i.

claim: In the mouse dataset, the pooled average of event number was significantly higher in the non-detected trials (right-tailed paired t-test, p=0.034), and trended towards significance in the human detection dataset (p=0.075).
source: In the mouse dataset, the pooled average of event number was significantly higher in the non-detected trials (right-tailed paired t-test, p=0.034), and trended towards significance in the human detection dataset (p=0.075).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of timing matched data shown in Figure 9ii.

claim: These results provide support for the hypothesis that event number can be predictive of detection independent of event timing.
source: Hence, these results provide support for the hypothesis that event number can be predictive of detection independent of event timing.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the timing matching analysis shown in Figure 9ii.

claim: The IEI distributions did not differ between detected versus non-detected or attend-in versus attend-out conditions.
source: The IEI distributions did not differ between detected versus non-detected or attend-in versus attend-out conditions (Figure 10i).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 10i.

claim: There was no clear evidence in the IEI distribution that beta events occur rhythmically in 1 s prestimulus windows.
source: Moreover, there was no clear evidence in the IEI distribution that beta events occur rhythmically in 1 s prestimulus windows.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the IEI distributions shown in Figure 10i.

claim: Many of the IEIs were concentrated at <150 ms, while a typical event duration was ~150 ms.
source: Figure 10i shows that many of the IEIs were concentrated at <150 ms, while a typical event duration was ~150 ms (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 10i and 5.

claim: This result suggests there were cases where multiple events occurred within one continuous high-power region (i.e. above the power cutoff).
source: This result suggests there were cases where multiple events occurred within one continuous high-power region (i.e. above the power cutoff, see Figure 2ii for examples).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the IEI and event duration data.

claim: Most supra-cutoff regions had a single local maximum (~80%) and the probability of a given number of maxima per event was not significantly different across behavioral conditions.
source: Most supra-cutoff regions had a single local maximum (~80%) and the probability of a given number of maxima per event was not significantly different across behavioral conditions (Figure 11i).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 11i.

claim: Multi-maxima events did not constitute a distinct class of events, with respect to how they influenced behavior.
source: This suggests that multi-maxima events did not constitute a distinct class of events, with respect to how they influenced behavior.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data in Figure 11i showing no difference across behavioral conditions.

claim: Successive supra-cutoff temporal regions were by definition separated by periods below the power cutoff, which effectively created a refractory period in the IEI histogram of 'non-overlapping events'.
source: Successive supra-cutoff temporal regions were by definition separated by periods below the power cutoff, which effectively created a refractory period in the IEI histogram of 'non-overlapping events' (Figure 11ii).
evidence: This is an inference about the cause of the IEI distribution shape shown in Figure 11ii.

claim: Neither the detected nor the non-detected (and, attend-in nor attend-out) IEI distributions were distinct from the jittered distributions, suggesting that 'non-overlapping beta events' did not occur rhythmically in any behavioral condition.
source: Neither the detected nor the non-detected (and, attend-in nor attend-out) IEI distributions were distinct from the jittered distributions, suggesting that 'non-overlapping beta events' did not occur rhythmically in any behavioral condition.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparison of IEI distributions with jittered distributions shown in Figure 11ii.

claim: This further corroborates the conclusion that beta event generation is not rhythmic.
source: This further corroborates the conclusion that beta event generation is not rhythmic.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the non-overlapping events analysis.

claim: Results on the relationships between beta event features and power and behavior also held under the 'non-overlapping events' definition, such that event number showed the highest correlation with mean prestimulus power and was the most consistent predictor of detection/attention.
source: Results on the relationships between beta event features and power and behavior also held under the 'non-overlapping events' definition, such that event number showed the highest correlation with mean prestimulus power (Figure 11iii) and was the most consistent predictor of detection/attention (Figure 11iv).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 11iii-iv.

claim: In all three datasets ~ 80% of non-overlapping events have only one local maximum, meaning they were also considered to be an event in the original definition.
source: This high congruency can be attributed to the fact that, as stated above, in all three datasets ~ 80% of non-overlapping events have only one local maximum, meaning they were also considered to be an event in the original definition.
evidence: This is an inference explaining the consistency between the two event definitions.

claim: The lack of evidence for rhythmicity of beta events, together with the Fano Factors being well over 1, implies that the underlying mechanism generating beta events was less regular than a Poisson process and more akin to a 'bursty' process.
source: The lack of evidence for rhythmicity of beta events (Figure 10i and Figure 11ii), together with the Fano Factors being well over 1 (Figure 10ii), implies that the underlying mechanism generating beta events was less regular than a Poisson process and more akin to a 'bursty' process.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data in Figures 10 and 11.

claim: A Dynamic Amplitude Modulation hypothesis predicts the existence of an ongoing continuous rhythm whose amplitude (and hence power) was dynamically modulated.
source: A Dynamic Amplitude Modulation hypothesis predicts the existence of an ongoing continuous rhythm whose amplitude (and hence power) was dynamically modulated.
evidence: This is a description of a hypothesis being tested.

claim: Under the Dynamic Amplitude Modulation hypothesis, the rhythmicity of the beta component of the signal would be independent of its amplitude.
source: Under this hypothesis, the rhythmicity of the beta component of the signal would be independent of its amplitude.
evidence: This is a prediction of the Dynamic Amplitude Modulation hypothesis.

claim: The Bursty Generator hypothesis assumes that the generator that triggers the beta waveform also causes the transient surge in beta amplitude.
source: In contrast, the Bursty Generator hypothesis assumes that the generator that triggers the beta waveform also causes the transient surge in beta amplitude.
evidence: This is a description of an alternative hypothesis being tested.

claim: Under the Bursty Generator hypothesis, beta rhythmicity is only present when this generator triggers the system: If so, rhythmicity would be restricted to high beta power regions of the data.
source: Under this hypothesis, beta rhythmicity is only present when this generator triggers the system: If so, rhythmicity would be restricted to high beta power regions of the data.
evidence: This is a prediction of the Bursty Generator hypothesis.

claim: Time lags above cutoff are integer multiples of the beta period (i.e. distributions are centered at 0), in direct contrast to time lags below cutoff that are not (i.e. distributions are flat).
source: These probability histograms show that time lags above cutoff are integer multiples of the beta period (i.e. distributions are centered at 0), in direct contrast to time lags below cutoff that are not (i.e. distributions are flat).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 12B.

claim: These results strongly support the prediction that high power regions are rhythmic but low power regions are not, providing evidence for the Bursty Generator hypothesis over the Dynamic Amplitude Modulation hypothesis.
source: Overall, these results strongly support the prediction that high power regions are rhythmic but low power regions are not, providing evidence for the Bursty Generator hypothesis over the Dynamic Amplitude Modulation hypothesis
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data in Figure 12B.

claim: Averaged prestimulus beta activity in somatosensory neocortex is predictive of perceptual success and shifts in attention, such that higher power reflects decreased detection or attention.
source: Our data showed that averaged prestimulus beta activity in somatosensory neocortex is predictive of perceptual success and shifts in attention, such that higher power reflects decreased detection or attention.
evidence: This is a summary of findings supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: This result held across various analysis methods, species and recording modalities (human MEG, mouse LFP).
source: This result held across various analysis methods, species and recording modalities (human MEG, mouse LFP)
evidence: This is a summary of findings supported by data throughout the results section.

claim: This result is consistent with the general prediction that spontaneous sensorimotor beta acts as, or is the by-product of, an 'inhibitory' process.
source: consistent with the general prediction that spontaneous sensorimotor beta acts as, or is the by-product of, an 'inhibitory' process (Engel and Fries, 2010; Haegens et al., 2011; Jones et al., 2010; Linkenkaer-Hansen et al., 2004).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the findings to prior theoretical frameworks, supported by citations.

claim: On individual trials, beta emerged as a brief high-power transient above background noise in the frequency spectrum and was consistent with a 'bursty' process as opposed to dynamic amplitude modulation of a sustained beta oscillation.
source: On individual trials, beta emerged as a brief high-power transient above background noise in the frequency spectrum and was consistent with a 'bursty' process as opposed to dynamic amplitude modulation of a sustained beta oscillation.
evidence: This is a summary of findings supported by data in Figures 2, 10, 11, and 12.

claim: The rate of prestimulus beta events was the most consistent predictor of detection and shifts in attention, and most strongly correlated with average prestimulus beta power.
source: Our results showed that the rate of prestimulus beta events was the most consistent predictor of detection and shifts in attention, and most strongly correlated with average prestimulus beta power.
evidence: This is a summary of findings supported by data in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: In human data, only the rate of events was significantly predictive of function across detection and attention tasks.
source: In human data, only the rate of events was significantly predictive of function across detection and attention tasks.
evidence: This is a summary of findings supported by data in Figure 7.

claim: An event occurring closer to the stimulus onset was more likely to result in non-detection.
source: Moreover, an event occurring closer to the stimulus onset was more likely to result in non-detection.
evidence: This is a summary of findings supported by data in Figure 8.

claim: Analysis of a subset of the data where the number of events, or conversely the timing of the 'most recent beta event', were matched across detected and non-detected trials showed that event number and timing may be independently informative to perception.
source: Analysis of a subset of the data where the number of events, or conversely the timing of the 'most recent beta event', were matched across detected and non-detected trials showed that event number and timing may be independently informative to perception.
evidence: This is a summary of findings supported by data in Figure 9.

claim: With shifts in attention, the brain decreases the probability of high-power beta events, and this decrease translates to improved sensory processing in the aligned sensory channel.
source: Taken together, our findings indicate that with shifts in attention, the brain decreases the probability of high-power beta events, and this decrease translates to improved sensory processing in the aligned sensory channel.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the attention task data.

claim: These are the first results to show that rate of beta events in human neocortical signals is a meaningful predictor of function.
source: To our knowledge, these are the first results to show that rate of beta events in human neocortical signals is a meaningful predictor of function.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: Prior studies in animal models have shown that features of transient beta activity in LFP signals correlate with behavior, including motor and cognitive and working memory processes.
source: Prior studies in animal models have shown that features of transient beta activity in LFP signals correlate with behavior, including motor and cognitive (Bartolo and Merchant, 2015; Feingold et al., 2015) and working memory processes (Lundqvist et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Homology in beta event characteristics across tasks, recording modalities, and species, suggests modulation of beta event rate may be the fundamental feature underlying behaviorally relevant differences in averaged beta power.
source: Homology in beta event characteristics across tasks, recording modalities, and species, suggests modulation of beta event rate may be the fundamental feature underlying behaviorally relevant differences in averaged beta power.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the consistency of findings across datasets.

claim: A well-established theory suggests a crucial role for the specific alignment of oscillatory phases with external input, with specific phases beneficial for signal transmission while others are not.
source: A well-established theory suggests a crucial role for the specific alignment of oscillatory phases with external input, with specific phases beneficial for signal transmission while others are not (Bastos et al., 2015; Lakatos et al., 2007; Schroeder et al., 2008; van Elswijk et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: In spontaneous, prestimulus, anticipatory states it is unlikely that beta's local influence on the filtering of sensory input is through a temporal phase-alignment code.
source: In contrast, our current study suggests that in spontaneous, prestimulus, anticipatory states it is unlikely that beta's local influence on the filtering of sensory input is through a temporal phase-alignment code.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the findings about beta event rate and timing.

claim: In all three of our tasks, the precise timing of the sensory stimulus onset is unpredictable for the subject (i.e. randomized design).
source: Rather, in all three of our tasks, the precise timing of the sensory stimulus onset is unpredictable for the subject (i.e. randomized design).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Under these conditions, our results suggest that the inhibitory correlation between beta and perception may reflect the presence of another process that enhances beta event probability/rate, such as an increase in a specific thalamic input and/or the existence of a specific neuromodulatory environment that promotes this rhythm.
source: Under these conditions, our results suggest that the inhibitory correlation between beta and perception may reflect the presence of another process that enhances beta event probability/rate, such as an increase in a specific thalamic input and/or the existence of a specific neuromodulatory environment that promotes this rhythm.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms underlying the findings.

claim: If a single beta event occurs within 200 ms before the sensory stimulus, the stimulus is less likely to be perceived, suggesting that the increased rate in non-attended conditions acts to increase the probability that an event will occur close to, or perhaps during, the stimulus.
source: Further, if a single beta event occurs within 200 ms before the sensory stimulus, the stimulus is less likely to be perceived, suggesting that the increased rate in non-attended conditions acts to increase the probability that an event will occur close to, or perhaps during, the stimulus.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the timing analysis in Figure 8.

claim: Beta events could have an inhibitory impact on function for a prolonged period that extends longer than the event duration, a period that could be as long as 200 ms.
source: In this case, beta events could have an inhibitory impact on function for a prolonged period that extends longer than the event duration, a period that could be as long as 200 ms.
evidence: This is speculation about the temporal extent of beta events' functional impact.

claim: This finding does not preclude a role for band-band phase-coherence between brain regions in information processing.
source: Of note, this finding does not preclude a role for band-band phase-coherence between brain regions in information processing (Sacchet et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a clarification about the scope of the findings, supported by citation.

claim: Our results are relevant to the potential interpretation of phase of a local spontaneous beta 'oscillation' at the timing of external stimulus arrival and suggest that the beta's inhibitory influence is likely not due to a specific phase-alignment.
source: Rather, our results are relevant to the potential interpretation of phase of a local spontaneous beta 'oscillation' at the timing of external stimulus arrival and suggest that the beta's inhibitory influence is likely not due to a specific phase-alignment.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of the findings for phase-alignment theories.

claim: Our findings directly indicate that the circuit-level mechanisms that create beta events recruit an 'inhibitory' process that decreases the relay of sensory information to or from SI.
source: Our findings directly indicate that the circuit-level mechanisms that create beta events recruit an 'inhibitory' process that decreases the relay of sensory information to or from SI.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanistic implications of the findings.

claim: The rate of beta events therefore predicts the presence of this inhibitory process at the time of the stimulus.
source: The rate of beta events therefore predicts the presence of this inhibitory process at the time of the stimulus.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the relationship between event rate and detection.

claim: Converging evidence in humans and animals supported a model-derived theory that the circuit-mechanisms creating high-power beta events consisted of bursts of subthreshold excitatory synaptic drive targeting proximal and distal dendrites of pyramidal neurons, such that the distal drive was effectively stronger and lasted ~50 ms.
source: Converging evidence in humans and animals supported a model-derived theory that the circuit-mechanisms creating high-power beta events consisted of bursts of subthreshold excitatory synaptic drive targeting proximal and distal dendrites of pyramidal neurons, such that the distal drive was effectively stronger and lasted ~50 ms.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Sherman et al., 2016).

claim: Our present study implies that beta's inhibitory impact on function is largely related to the likelihood of observing this strong distal drive (event number) and/or the strong distal drive happening closer to the onset of the stimulus ('most recent event' timing), in contrast to stronger distal drive (event power), longer lasting drive (event duration) or drive covering a larger frequency span in the spectrogram (event frequency span).
source: Our present study implies that beta's inhibitory impact on function is largely related to the likelihood of observing this strong distal drive (event number) and/or the strong distal drive happening closer to the onset of the stimulus ('most recent event' timing), in contrast to stronger distal drive (event power), longer lasting drive (event duration) or drive covering a larger frequency span in the spectrogram (event frequency span).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the current findings to prior mechanistic work.

claim: The strong distal drive to SI could decrease the efficacy of information processing by supragranular inputs to SI through recruitment of inhibitory neurons in supragranular layers.
source: First, the strong distal drive to SI could decrease the efficacy of information processing by supragranular inputs to SI. One prominent candidate for this mechanism is recruitment of inhibitory neurons in supragranular layers (Jones et al., 2009).
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms, supported by citation.

claim: Such inputs could also alter distal dendritic processes in large layer V neurons, the primary contributor to the MEG signals recorded.
source: Such inputs could also alter distal dendritic processes in large layer V neurons (Larkum, 2013; Murphy et al., 2016; Takahashi et al., 2016), the primary contributor to the MEG signals recorded.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms, supported by citations.

claim: The generators of the exogenous drive contributing to beta emergence in SI (e.g. bursting in thalamic neurons) could themselves mediate beta's inhibitory impact on perception at the locale of the exogenous generator (e.g. through a filtering process in the thalamus), in which case the increase in neocortical beta events represents an epiphenominal reflection of this process.
source: Alternatively, the generators of the exogenous drive contributing to beta emergence in SI (e.g. bursting in thalamic neurons) could themselves mediate beta's inhibitory impact on perception at the locale of the exogenous generator (e.g. through a filtering process in the thalamus), in which case the increase in neocortical beta events represents an epiphenominal reflection of this process.
evidence: This is speculation about an alternative mechanism.

claim: The mechanisms of generation of high-power beta events may be distinct from lower-power beta transients, and thus separable in their impact on function.
source: Based on the following, we conjecture that the mechanisms of generation of high-power beta events may be distinct from lower-power beta transients, and thus separable in their impact on function.
evidence: This is speculation based on the following evidence presented.

claim: High power beta events were stereotyped in their waveforms and in their spectral features, i.e. the event duration and frequency span.
source: First, high power beta events were stereotyped in their waveforms (Sherman et al., 2016) and in their spectral features, i.e. the event duration and frequency span (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Despite the lack of clear bimodality in the full distribution of beta event power, there was a clear switch in the relative importance of event features as the beta event power cutoff was varied.
source: Second, sliding power cutoff analyses showed that despite the lack of clear bimodality in the full distribution of beta event power, there was a clear switch in the relative importance of event features as the beta event power cutoff was varied.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figures 6—figure supplement 2 and 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: For lower power cutoffs (<~3X median) beta event power is more predictive of averaged prestimulus power and behavior than beta event rate, while for higher cutoffs (>3X median) beta event rate is more predictive.
source: For lower power cutoffs (<~3X median) beta event power is more predictive of averaged prestimulus power and behavior than beta event rate, while for higher cutoffs (>3X median) beta event rate is more predictive.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figures 6—figure supplement 2 and 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The intervals between consecutive high power beta events were consistent with a bursty process, as opposed to dynamic amplitude modulation of a continuous process.
source: Third, we found that the intervals between consecutive high power beta events were consistent with a bursty process, as opposed to dynamic amplitude modulation of a continuous process.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figures 10, 11, and 12.

claim: The mechanisms underlying the high-power beta events that dominate fluctuations in the averaged prestimulus beta power are distinct in their generation and relationship to function.
source: Taken together, our prior (Sherman et al., 2016) and current results suggest that the mechanisms underlying the high-power beta events that dominate fluctuations in the averaged prestimulus beta power are distinct in their generation and relationship to function.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the current and prior findings.

claim: Transient rhythms emerging for a few cycles have been reported in other bands, including gamma and alpha.
source: Indeed, transient rhythms emerging for a few cycles have been reported in other bands, including gamma (Burns et al., 2011; Greenwood et al., 2015; Lundqvist et al., 2016) and alpha (Jones et al., 2009; Sherman et al., 2016; Ziegler et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The bump in the beta band emerges primarily between 18–22 Hz, also known as the beta 2 range, and we do not observe a separate bump for the beta 1 range (typically ~15 Hz).
source: The bump in the beta band emerges primarily between 18–22 Hz, also known as the beta 2 range, and we do not observe a separate bump for the beta 1 range (typically ~15 Hz; [Kopell et al., 2014]).
evidence: This is an observation about the spectral characteristics of the data, with citation.

claim: This isolated increase in the power spectral density in the beta band is indicative of a singular underlying mechanism.
source: We conjecture that this isolated increase in the power spectral density in the beta band is indicative of a singular underlying mechanism.
evidence: This is speculation based on the spectral characteristics.

claim: We have previously shown evidence for a unique mechanism that generates stereotyped and homogeneous beta-band activity.
source: In further support, as discussed above, we have previously shown evidence for a unique mechanism that generates stereotyped and homogeneous beta-band activity (Sherman et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Our data also show high power alpha band activity.
source: Of note, our data also show high power alpha band activity (Jones et al., 2010; Jones et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: We have observed that alpha and beta have separable correlations with attention and perception.
source: We have observed that alpha and beta have separable correlations with attention and perception.
evidence: This is a statement about prior observations.

claim: Shifts in averaged alpha power occur sooner after attentional cues than shifts in beta power, and beta showed a stronger linear relationship to detectability.
source: Shifts in averaged alpha power occur sooner after attentional cues than shifts in beta power, and beta showed a stronger linear relationship to detectability (Jones et al., 2010; Sacchet et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The transient nature of high-power spontaneous beta events observed here has direct implications for brain stimulation studies, such as transcranial alternating current (tACS) or magnetic stimulation (TMS), aimed at entraining 'rhythms' to causally modulate behavior.
source: The transient nature of high-power spontaneous beta events observed here has direct implications for brain stimulation studies, such as transcranial alternating current (tACS) or magnetic stimulation (TMS), aimed at entraining 'rhythms' to causally modulate behavior.
evidence: This is speculation about the implications of the findings for brain stimulation.

claim: Causal manipulations may be more effective if they are designed to match the intermittent character and specific temporal characteristics of the beta events observed.
source: Causal manipulations may be more effective if they are designed to match the intermittent character and specific temporal characteristics of the beta events observed.
evidence: This is speculation about how to design effective brain stimulation protocols.

claim: Our results suggest the rate and timing of beta events is a key target for modulation.
source: Our results suggest the rate and timing of beta events is a key target for modulation.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of the findings for brain stimulation.

claim: Stimulation protocols that drive two or more events in the 1 s prestimulus period may impair perception, whereas blocking such events may benefit perception.
source: Specifically, stimulation protocols that drive two or more events in the 1 s prestimulus period may impair perception, whereas blocking such events may benefit perception.
evidence: This is speculation about specific stimulation protocols based on the findings.

claim: Our data predict that driving single events could impair throughput in the aligned somatotopic area, but only if it arrives close to the time of the stimulus.
source: Our data predict that driving single events could impair throughput in the aligned somatotopic area, but only if it arrives close to the time of the stimulus.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the timing findings.

claim: Cumulative evidence across tasks, recording modalities, and species support the notion that as opposed to phase-alignment, amplitude modulation, sustained rhythmicity or several other possible means by which transient, high-power beta events could influence behavior (e.g. frequency span), beta event rate has a dominant impact on function.
source: In summary, cumulative evidence across tasks, recording modalities, and species support the notion that as opposed to phase-alignment, amplitude modulation, sustained rhythmicity or several other possible means by which transient, high-power beta events could influence behavior (e.g. frequency span), beta event rate has a dominant impact on function.
evidence: This is a summary inference drawn from all the findings.
